newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weary Mir crew plunge station into new crisis.
newsitem.headline: Weary Mir crew plunge station into new crisis.

text.p: A weary cosmonaut aboard Russia's Mir space station mistakenly pulled out a vital computer cable on Thursday, plunging the crippled ship into darkness and its worst crisis since a near-fatal collision three weeks ago.

The three-man crew, whose commander developed a probably stress-induced heart problem this week, had to sit in their Soyuz escape capsule to communicate with Earth and were using flashlights to get around the darkened station.

"I should stress it is an especially unpleasant situation. It very much recalls the situation we were in after the crash," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow.
A spokesman later denied Russian news agency reports that the crew would have to abandon ship by 1000 GMT on Friday if attempts to recharge batteries failed and fuel ran low on Soyuz.

The cosmonauts were in no immediate danger from the latest in this year's jinx-like series of Mir mishaps and had no plans to abandon ship, Solovyov insisted, even though light, heating and life-support systems were shut down on the main station.

The crew have canned oxygen for just five days, while the temperature and humidity will remain bearable for two or three days without power. That sets a clear time limit on re-starting Mir's life-support machines, including the oxygen generators.
Deputy mission director Viktor Blagov said he was confident the problems would be sorted out.
A Mission Control spokesman later said the Friday deadline cited by Russian news agencies "does not correspond to reality".

At issue is how fast Mir's batteries can accumulate the electric power to jolt the disabled gyroscopic navigation system back into action and how fast the cosmonauts burn up rocket fuel in Soyuz's engines, which they are firing to keep Mir's solar panels lined up on the Sun in the absence of the gyroscopes.

If, before the batteries were charged, fuel fell to a level where there was only enough left to get Soyuz back to Earth, then the crew would depart, officials said. But the spokesman said Soyuz was burning little fuel and had plenty left.
"We've always succeeded before," Blagov told reporters.
Meanwhile, the crew even had orders to go on preparing for a risky repair to electric cables damaged in the June 25 accident -- though privately officials said its now likely to be put off.

The tension was palpable at Mission Control in the biggest drama since last month's collision -- also possibly caused by a crew error -- which cut power by up to half and nearly cost the men their lives when one of Mir's modules was holed.
"This is a kindergarten!" a frustrated Solovyov said aloud after telling the crew repeatedly to shut down systems.

"This was purely human error," he told reporters of the latest crisis. Officials have neither confirmed nor denied reports that a basic mistake by Tsibliyev caused the collision nor a Tass report that it was he who made Thursday's mistake.

Commander Tsibliyev, 43, was pulled from the two-man repair team on Wednesday after developing an irregular heartbeat. Doctors said on Thursday that his health had not deteriorated. But NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, is now due to step in to a spacesuit to help flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39.
But they have just an hour of daylight during every two-hour orbit to continue preparations. And with signs of fatigue showing up in mistakes, the repair schedule was in doubt.

Russian officials said the job may well now be left for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7 -- if Mir is still habitable. If the present crew abandoned ship, Mir would die as its systems cannot operate without human hands on the controls.

The original collision was the worst accident in its 11 years in space but by no means an isolated mishap, and had already raised questions over whether it should be ditched before a new international space station is launched next year.
Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they do not want to abandon the station.

U.S. President Bill Clinton said: "As far as we know right now, they have gotten control of things and there seems to be no immediate crisis." But if things become untenable, the Mir crew will fly the Soyuz escape capsule home.
Back on Earth British-born Foale's mother was keeping a stiff upper lip. "We are concerned," she said. "But not unduly."
